newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris reconsiders Algerian Islamic threat.
newsitem.headline: Paris reconsiders Algerian Islamic threat.

text.p: A bomb that tore through a Paris train has left French anti-terrorism investigators wondering whether the authorities brushed off too soon the Algerian Moslem fundamentalist threat.

The bomb that killed two people and injured 79 others at the Port Royal regional express station on Tuesday bore all the hallmarks of last year's bombings by Algerian fundamentalists -- similar target, timing and explosive device.

The newspaper Le Monde said France's DST counter-espionage service had warned the government in early November that an Algerian militant was on his way from Afghanistan to carry out attacks on French interests, but French agents lost his trail.

In January, Algerian secret services told their French counterparts that a commando of Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA) might be about to arrive in France. Paris authorities, which had been misled by Algiers several times, treated the report with scepticism.
French authorites claimed victory after the attacks which killed eight people in Paris and Lyon last year when more than 100 suspected fundamentalist supporters were rounded-up in police raids.
"Networks which represented an immediate and fearsome danger for our country have been dismantled," Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said in March after scores of arrests.

Since the last bombing in October, Debre had ordered a gradual easing of a security alert codenamed Vigipirate which involved police and army patrols, and searches, at sensitive spots including stations, airports and tourist sites.
Within hours of Tuesday's blast, Prime Minister Alain Juppe had reimposed the security measures.

Anti-terrorism investigating magistrates complain they have not been able to bring more cases to trial partly because of differing legal procedures or reluctance to cooperate from European partners including Germany, Britain and Belgium.

Last week, a senior judicial source was looking forward to the start of France's first trial of fundamentalists next Monday -- a ring that recruited youngsters in French inner-cities for planned attacks in north Africa.
"It's an exemplary case, it will explain many things about these people's motivations and ideology, their idea of the jihad (Holy War)," the source, who asked for anonymity, told Reuters.
"Today these networks are increasingly migrating northwards, to Britain, Nordic countries, and North America," he said, although he cautioned that there was still a risk in France.
In the first case to reach court, 34 suspected members of a ring dismantled following a series of attacks in Morocco in August 1994, will stand trial on charges of terrorist conspiracy from Monday.

Investigators say the ring recruited, indoctrinated and trained in military camps in Algeria or Afghanistan young people from Paris, Orleans and Besancon to spread the Jihad in Morocco and across North Africa.
